transcript.content: Hello, welcome in. To start, can you tell me what brings you in to see me today?

Well, hi. Thank you for seeing me. I, uh, I guess I'm here because things have just been getting really... noticeable, I suppose. I mean, I work in customer service, right? Taking calls all day, which is draining enough on its own, but lately, it's like my body just isn't cooperating with me at all, and people are actually starting to point it out. 

Like, my supervisor or even just friends who come over, they can actually see me doing this. Half the time, it's like I'm moving like I'm underwater. Everything is just so heavy and slow. I'll sit there and it takes me absolutely forever just to formulate an answer to a simple question, or even just to physically push myself out of a chair to go to the kitchen. It's this deep, heavy drag, like gravity is turned up. 

But then, on the flip side—and this is the part that really made me think I needed to come in—sometimes it's the exact opposite. I'll be in my apartment after a shift, and I just can't stop moving. I'll be pacing back and forth across the living room, just walking holes into the carpet, rubbing my hands together over and over. It's almost like... you know when you get a really bad, screaming customer on the line and you just need to shake off that bad call? It's exactly like I'm trying to physically shake that off, but it's happening all the time, even when I haven't taken a call. And people are looking at me like I'm acting bizarre, pointing out how restless or how sluggish I am, so... yeah, that's really why I made the appointment. I just can't seem to find a normal speed anymore.
Aside from these changes in your movement and energy, have you also been feeling persistently sad, down, or empty most of the day?

Sad? No, not really. I mean, it's funny you ask that because my mom actually called me last week—she usually calls on Sunday evenings just to catch up, you know, ask about how the calls are going at work and everything—and she asked me almost the exact same thing. She was like, "Are you feeling depressed?" because I guess I just sounded so incredibly flat and slow on the phone with her. But I had to tell her, and I'll tell you too, it's really not sadness. 

I don't sit around crying or feeling empty inside, like, at all. I don't have that heavy, dark emotional cloud over my head that people always talk about when they're down in the dumps. It's really just... well, exactly like I was saying before, it's this physical drag or this physical restlessness. I still care about things, you know? I still watch my shows—I've actually been rewatching this whole sci-fi series from the early 2000s after my shifts, and I still get totally invested in the plot and the characters and everything. 

So the emotional part, the sadness or feeling hollowed out... no, I don't feel that. If I was sad, I feel like I'd definitely know it, right? Because I've been sad before, like when I had to drop a couple of classes back in college or when I've gone through breakups, and this doesn't feel anything like that. This is just... I don't know, my brain and my body just not syncing up right on a physical level. But emotionally? No, I wouldn't say I feel down or empty during the day. Just frustrated by the moving slow or pacing around part, really.
Are you currently taking, or have you recently started, any antipsychotic medications or other new prescription drugs?

Medications? No, no, I am not taking anything like that. I mean, honestly, I am not really a big pill person to begin with. The most I ever take is maybe some ibuprofen if I get a headache, which, to be fair, happens pretty often at work because those headsets they give us for the calls are so incredibly tight. They just clamp down on your ears and by hour six, your head is just throbbing right at the temples, you know? But even then, I try to just drink a big glass of water instead of taking anything if I can help it. 

So as far as prescriptions go, or antipsychotics, which sounds really intense, honestly, no, I haven't started anything new. I haven't been to a doctor for a prescription in... wow, I do not even know how long. Maybe a few years back when I had strep throat? I had to take antibiotics for that, and even that was a whole ordeal because I kept forgetting to take them at the exact same time every day with food, and you know how they always tell you to finish the whole bottle even if you feel better? I am terrible at that, I always just stop when my throat stops hurting. 

But yeah, recently? Nothing at all. My medicine cabinet in the bathroom is basically just toothpaste, some old allergy pills from last spring when the pollen was really bad, and a box of bandaids. I don't even take a daily vitamin right now, though my mom is always getting on my case about that too, telling me I need more vitamin D since I'm inside taking calls all day. So no, nothing new, and definitely no prescription drugs whatsoever.
Have you noticed anything unusual lately, like hearing voices or sounds other people don't seem to hear, or having thoughts or beliefs that others have told you seem strange or untrue?

Well, it's funny you mention the hearing things part, because... I don't know if I'd call it a voice exactly, like a ghost or something, but... yeah, there's this thing that keeps happening. And it's actually been driving me a little crazy, to be honest. 

So, you know how I mentioned I work in customer service? We use this software system on our laptops, and every time a new call comes into the queue, there's this very specific, sharp little double-beep in the headset. It's designed to be annoying so you don't miss it, right? Well, lately, I've been hearing it when I'm completely off the clock. I'll be in my apartment, my laptop will be shut—completely powered down, sitting on the kitchen counter—and I'll hear that exact beep. Clear as day. 

And it's not just the beep, either. Sometimes, right after it, I'll hear this voice. It sounds just like one of the floor supervisors, you know, that really clipped, impatient tone they get when the hold times are too long? And it just says my name, or it'll say, "Too slow." Just like that. "Too slow." And the first few times it happened, I actually jumped up. I thought, 'Oh my god, did I leave my work laptop open? Am I logged in?' I went tearing into the kitchen, opening the laptop, checking my status, but of course, it was off. 

It happens when I'm just trying to relax, like when I'm watching that sci-fi show I told you about. I'll be right in the middle of a really good episode, and then... *beep beep*... "Too slow." And I'll pause the TV and look around, and my apartment is completely silent. It's just me. But it sounds so real, like someone is standing right behind my left shoulder, just over my ear. I even asked my buddy Mark when he was over last week—we were having a beer on the couch, and I heard it, and I was like, "Dude, did you hear that?" And he just looked at me like I had two heads. He was like, "Hear what? The fridge running?" 

So, yeah... I guess I am hearing something that other people aren't. But it's so specific to work, you know? It's not like a random stranger, it's that supervisor voice and that stupid beep. It's like I can't leave the job at the office, even when everything is unplugged. I don't know if that's what you mean by unusual, but it's definitely been happening a lot lately.
Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, fevers, seizures, or been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions around the time these movement changes and voices started?

Illnesses or head injuries? No, honestly, my physical health has been totally fine. I mean, knock on wood, right? I'm actually one of those people who almost never gets sick. Like, at the call center, it's basically a giant petri dish because everyone is sitting in these tiny cubicles that are practically right on top of each other, and the ventilation in that building is just terrible. I swear they never change the air filters. Just last month, half my team was out with some awful stomach bug or maybe it was the flu, I don't even know, they were all just coughing and calling out sick left and right. The supervisor was freaking out about coverage. But me? I didn't catch a single thing. Not even a slight fever or the sniffles. I haven't had a fever since... man, probably that time I got that strep throat a few years ago that I was telling you about earlier. So definitely no recent illnesses or fevers or anything like that going around the time this all started. 

And head injuries? No, definitely not. I mean, I can be pretty clumsy sometimes, I'll admit that. Like, I'll stub my toe on the coffee table, or just last week I actually bumped my shoulder pretty hard on the doorframe when I was rushing to grab my food delivery from the hall, but I definitely haven't hit my head. No concussions, no falling down, no car accidents, nothing like that at all. 

And seizures? Oh, wow, no, that sounds terrifying. I had a dog growing up that had seizures and it was incredibly scary to watch, but no, I've never had a seizure in my life, thankfully. And since I haven't been to a regular doctor in ages anyway, there's definitely no new medical conditions or neurological diagnoses on my chart. Like I said before with the medication thing, I don't even go to the doctor for checkups, so I'm definitely not managing any kind of physical illness or anything like that. My body, health-wise, is completely normal, aside from that weird pacing and moving slow stuff I mentioned earlier. But yeah, no fevers, no head trauma, no seizures, nothing physical like that at all.
How long ago did these symptoms—the slowed or restless movements and the beeping/voice you hear—first start, and have they been continuous or getting worse since then?

Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it's actually been quite a while. I know I was talking earlier about the headsets and the cubicles and the supervisors like I'm still sitting in that chair every single day, because honestly, that's exactly how it feels in my head, but... I actually don't work there anymore. I was fired. So this whole thing, the weird pacing around my apartment, the feeling like my limbs are made of lead, and definitely the beeping and that supervisor's voice... it all started right after I was let go from that customer-support job. 

It's been about two years and three months now. I remember the exact timeline because it was just such a massive shock to my system. I mean, they pulled me into this tiny little glass office—the one the shift managers use, right by the breakroom where the coffee machine is always broken—and HR was sitting there. You always know it's bad news when someone from HR is sitting there holding a manila folder. They told me my "average handle time" wasn't meeting their metrics, which felt incredibly unfair because I was actually trying to help the callers, not just rush them off the phone, you know? But they didn't care. They just took my keycard and escorted me out. 

And almost right after that, like within the first week of me just sitting at home on my couch, trying to figure out how I was going to pay rent and what I was supposed to do with my life, that's when all of this really started. I just couldn't sit still, I was pacing holes in my living room rug, just walking back and forth, and then other days I'd just feel so physically heavy and slow I could barely get up to get a glass of water from the kitchen. And the phantom beeping started right around then, too. 

As for whether it's continuous or getting worse... it really hasn't stopped once in that whole two years and three months. Not once. At first, I tried to rationalize it. I told myself it was just like when you've been on a boat all day and you still feel the waves when you're on dry land, you know? I figured it was just my brain holding onto the stress of the routine. But it never faded away like it's supposed to. If anything, it's definitely getting worse, or at least it feels louder and more frequent now. It used to just happen when I was stressing out about finding a new job or looking at my bank account, but now it interrupts me when I'm just trying to watch my sci-fi shows or eat dinner. It's just constant. Two years and three months of not being able to escape that place, even though I haven't logged into their system since the day they walked me out the door.
Do you have any family members—parents, siblings, or other close relatives—who have been diagnosed with schizophrenia or another psychotic illness?

Family history? Um, no, definitely not. I mean, if we are talking about schizophrenia or anything like that, no one in my family has ever had anything even close to that. My family is actually pretty boring, to be honest. Take my dad, for instance. He worked at the post office for thirty-two years, just retired last spring, and his biggest issue is that he gets a little grumpy if he misses his evening news. He spends all his time in the garage now building these elaborate birdhouses. And my mom, well, she can be a bit of a worrier, I guess. Like when I first moved into my apartment, she would call me twice a day just to make sure I locked the deadbolt and didn't leave the stove on, but that is just her being an overprotective mom, you know? She has never heard voices or had any kind of breakdown or anything. 

I also have an older sister, Chloe. She lives out in Oregon now, works as a dental hygienist. She is super organized, like, color-codes her entire life, which drives me a little crazy sometimes because I am definitely not like that, but she is totally healthy. We talk on the phone maybe once a month, usually on Sundays, and she is just living a totally normal life with her husband and their golden retriever. 

I think the only person who ever had any kind of brain issue was my grandma on my mom's side, but she was eighty-eight and had dementia right at the very end, which the doctors said was just from old age, so that doesn't really count, right? That is completely different. So yeah, I have racked my brain about this before, and it is really just me dealing with all this weird stuff. No family history of any psychotic illnesses at all.

I'll be in my apartment, my laptop will be shut—completely powered down, sitting on the kitchen counter—and I'll hear that exact beep. Clear as day. 

And it's not just the beep, either. Sometimes, right after it, I'll hear this voice. It sounds just like one of the floor supervisors, you know, that really clipped, impatient tone they get when the hold times are too long? And it just says my name, or it'll say, "Too slow." Just like that. "Too slow." And the first few times it happened, I actually jumped up. I thought, 'Oh my god, did I leave my work laptop open? Am I logged in?' I went tearing into the kitchen, opening the laptop, checking my status, but of course, it was off. 

It happens when I'm just trying to relax, like when I'm watching that sci-fi show I told you about. I'll be right in the middle of a really good episode, and then... *beep beep*... "Too slow." And I'll pause the TV and look around, and my apartment is completely silent. It's just me. But it sounds so real, like someone is standing right behind my left shoulder, just over my ear. I even asked my buddy Mark when he was over last week—we were having a beer on the couch, and I heard it, and I was like, "Dude, did you hear that?" And he just looked at me like I had two heads. He was like, "Hear what? The fridge running?" 

So, yeah... I guess I am hearing something that other people aren't. But it's so specific to work, you know? It's not like a random stranger, it's that supervisor voice and that stupid beep. It's like I can't leave the job at the office, even when everything is unplugged. I don't know if that's what you mean by unusual, but it's definitely been happening a lot lately.

inference.note: Patient explicitly denies sadness, emptiness, or depressive mood, making a mood (bipolar) etiology for the catatonic symptoms less likely, so F31.6 is removed. The persistent, context-specific auditory hallucinations (work-related beep and supervisor voice) combined with alternating stupor and excitement support ongoing consideration of a psychotic disorder (F20.2) or catatonia secondary to another medical/physiological condition (F06.1) pending further medical workup.

doctor.intent: Assess for an underlying general medical, neurological, or substance-related cause that could explain the catatonic symptoms and hallucinations (relevant to F06.1 vs F20.2)
doctor.question: Have you had any recent illnesses, head injuries, fevers, seizures, or been diagnosed with any medical or neurological conditions around the time these movement changes and voices started?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about recent illnesses, head injuries, seizures, or medical/neurological conditions to rule out general medical conditions causing the symptoms. My symptom profile does not contain an item for this.

patient.answer:
Illnesses or head injuries? No, honestly, my physical health has been totally fine. I mean, knock on wood, right? I'm actually one of those people who almost never gets sick. Like, at the call center, it's basically a giant petri dish because everyone is sitting in these tiny cubicles that are practically right on top of each other, and the ventilation in that building is just terrible. I swear they never change the air filters. Just last month, half my team was out with some awful stomach bug or maybe it was the flu, I don't even know, they were all just coughing and calling out sick left and right. The supervisor was freaking out about coverage. But me? I didn't catch a single thing. Not even a slight fever or the sniffles. I haven't had a fever since... man, probably that time I got that strep throat a few years ago that I was telling you about earlier. So definitely no recent illnesses or fevers or anything like that going around the time this all started. 

And head injuries? No, definitely not. I mean, I can be pretty clumsy sometimes, I'll admit that. Like, I'll stub my toe on the coffee table, or just last week I actually bumped my shoulder pretty hard on the doorframe when I was rushing to grab my food delivery from the hall, but I definitely haven't hit my head. No concussions, no falling down, no car accidents, nothing like that at all. 

And seizures? Oh, wow, no, that sounds terrifying. I had a dog growing up that had seizures and it was incredibly scary to watch, but no, I've never had a seizure in my life, thankfully. And since I haven't been to a regular doctor in ages anyway, there's definitely no new medical conditions or neurological diagnoses on my chart. Like I said before with the medication thing, I don't even go to the doctor for checkups, so I'm definitely not managing any kind of physical illness or anything like that. My body, health-wise, is completely normal, aside from that weird pacing and moving slow stuff I mentioned earlier. But yeah, no fevers, no head trauma, no seizures, nothing physical like that at all.

inference.note: Auditory hallucinations (work-related beep/voice) with catatonic-like motor symptoms (psychomotor retardation and agitation/stereotypies) reported, without depressive mood symptoms and no medication or medical/neurological cause identified, keeping both a medical/psychotic catatonia (F06.1) and catatonic schizophrenia (F20.2) as candidates. No new findings ruled out either option.

doctor.intent: Assess the total duration and course of the movement changes and auditory hallucinations to help distinguish a primary psychotic disorder (schizophrenia) from a catatonic syndrome due to an underlying medical condition
doctor.question: How long ago did these symptoms—the slowed or restless movements and the beeping/voice you hear—first start, and have they been continuous or getting worse since then?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on for about 2 years and 3 months, starting after I was fired from my customer-support job.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about when the symptoms (movements and hallucinations) first started, which corresponds to the overall duration of the illness.

patient.answer:
Well, if I really sit down and trace it back... it's actually been quite a while. I know I was talking earlier about the headsets and the cubicles and the supervisors like I'm still sitting in that chair every single day, because honestly, that's exactly how it feels in my head, but... I actually don't work there anymore. I was fired. So this whole thing, the weird pacing around my apartment, the feeling like my limbs are made of lead, and definitely the beeping and that supervisor's voice... it all started right after I was let go from that customer-support job. 

It's been about two years and three months now. I remember the exact timeline because it was just such a massive shock to my system. I mean, they pulled me into this tiny little glass office—the one the shift managers use, right by the breakroom where the coffee machine is always broken—and HR was sitting there. You always know it's bad news when someone from HR is sitting there holding a manila folder. They told me my "average handle time" wasn't meeting their metrics, which felt incredibly unfair because I was actually trying to help the callers, not just rush them off the phone, you know? But they didn't care. They just took my keycard and escorted me out. 

And almost right after that, like within the first week of me just sitting at home on my couch, trying to figure out how I was going to pay rent and what I was supposed to do with my life, that's when all of this really started. I just couldn't sit still, I was pacing holes in my living room rug, just walking back and forth, and then other days I'd just feel so physically heavy and slow I could barely get up to get a glass of water from the kitchen. And the phantom beeping started right around then, too. 

As for whether it's continuous or getting worse... it really hasn't stopped once in that whole two years and three months. Not once. At first, I tried to rationalize it. I told myself it was just like when you've been on a boat all day and you still feel the waves when you're on dry land, you know? I figured it was just my brain holding onto the stress of the routine. But it never faded away like it's supposed to. If anything, it's definitely getting worse, or at least it feels louder and more frequent now. It used to just happen when I was stressing out about finding a new job or looking at my bank account, but now it interrupts me when I'm just trying to watch my sci-fi shows or eat dinner. It's just constant. Two years and three months of not being able to escape that place, even though I haven't logged into their system since the day they walked me out the door.

inference.note: Duration of 2+ years with continuous auditory hallucinations (voice/beep) plus catatonic-like motor symptoms (stupor and agitation) without mood symptoms supports schizophrenia, catatonic type (F20.2). No medical/neurological illness, fever, head injury, or seizure identified, making a secondary catatonic disorder due to another medical condition (F06.1) less likely but not fully excluded pending further workup (e.g., labs, imaging). No evidence for substance-induced or mood-disorder-related catatonia.

doctor.intent: Assess for a family history of schizophrenia or other primary psychotic disorders, which would support a primary psychiatric etiology (F20.2) over a secondary catatonic disorder due to a general medical condition (F06.1)
doctor.question: Do you have any family members—parents, siblings, or other close relatives—who have been diagnosed with schizophrenia or another psychotic illness?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about family history of psychiatric illnesses, which is not covered by any item in my symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Family history? Um, no, definitely not. I mean, if we are talking about schizophrenia or anything like that, no one in my family has ever had anything even close to that. My family is actually pretty boring, to be honest. Take my dad, for instance. He worked at the post office for thirty-two years, just retired last spring, and his biggest issue is that he gets a little grumpy if he misses his evening news. He spends all his time in the garage now building these elaborate birdhouses. And my mom, well, she can be a bit of a worrier, I guess. Like when I first moved into my apartment, she would call me twice a day just to make sure I locked the deadbolt and didn't leave the stove on, but that is just her being an overprotective mom, you know? She has never heard voices or had any kind of breakdown or anything. 

I also have an older sister, Chloe. She lives out in Oregon now, works as a dental hygienist. She is super organized, like, color-codes her entire life, which drives me a little crazy sometimes because I am definitely not like that, but she is totally healthy. We talk on the phone maybe once a month, usually on Sundays, and she is just living a totally normal life with her husband and their golden retriever. 

I think the only person who ever had any kind of brain issue was my grandma on my mom's side, but she was eighty-eight and had dementia right at the very end, which the doctors said was just from old age, so that doesn't really count, right? That is completely different. So yeah, I have racked my brain about this before, and it is really just me dealing with all this weird stuff. No family history of any psychotic illnesses at all.

inference.note: No history of medical/neurological illness, head injury, fever, or seizures rules out organic catatonic disorder (F06.1). Chronic (>2 years) course with persistent catatonic-like motor symptoms (stupor alternating with excitement) plus mood-incongruent, work-themed auditory hallucinations, absence of depressive/manic symptoms, and no substance or medication cause supports schizophrenia, catatonic type (F20.2) as the primary diagnosis.
